title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes
seo_title: Year 5 Science: Reversible and Irreversible Changes Worksheets (Burning, Rusting, Fizzing)
standard_code: Year 5: Properties and changes of materials
standard_text: Demonstrate that dissolving, mixing and changes of state are reversible changes. Explain that some changes result in the formation of new materials, and that this kind of change is not usually reversible, including changes associated with burning and the action of acid on bicarbonate of soda.
meta_desc: Free Year 5 science worksheets on reversible and irreversible changes: melting, dissolving, burning, cooking, rusting, vinegar and bicarbonate of soda, and signs of new materials. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Melting and dissolving can be undone; burning and rusting make new materials.
body_html:
How to think about it

Some changes can be undone; others make new materials.

  • Reversible: melting, freezing, boiling, condensing, dissolving and mixing.
  • Irreversible: burning, cooking, rusting, and acids reacting with bicarbonate of soda. New materials are made.
  • Signs of a new material: gas bubbles, a lasting colour change, heat or light given out, a new smell.
Example

Toasting bread?

The bread changes colour and cannot change back

Answer: irreversible

Example

Melting butter?

It sets again when cooled

Answer: reversible

Common mistakes

  • Thinking melting is irreversible.
  • Thinking dissolving makes a new material.
  • Thinking iron rusts without water.

faq.q: What is the difference between reversible and irreversible changes?
faq.a: A reversible change, such as melting or dissolving, can be undone. An irreversible change, such as burning or cooking, makes new materials and cannot easily be undone.
Yes. The dissolved solid is still there and can be got back by evaporating the liquid.

faq.q: What happens when vinegar and bicarbonate of soda mix?
faq.a: They react and fizz, making carbon dioxide gas and new materials. It is an irreversible change.
